problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & ∗ \\ 2 & ∗\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $A=PD{P}^{-1},$ find the second column of the matrix $P.$

examples.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix Given Part of the Diagonalization
examples.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D=P^{-1}AP,$ find the value of $\dfrac{a}{b}.$
examples.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are $\lambda_1=5$ and $\lambda_2=-1.$

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_2=-1.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda_2=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get  

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the corresponding system of linear equations, we construct the augmented matrix $M$ and reduce it to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). So, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_1= -{2}x_2.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

By setting $x_2=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, $\dfrac{a}{b}=\dfrac{-2}{1} = -2.$

feedback.problem:
Determine if the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]$
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 1 \\ -1 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-1\cdot (-1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +9 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)(\lambda -3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=3.$ Since we get one repeated eigenvalue, the matrix might not be diagonalizable. To check this, we row-reduce the matrix $(A-3I)\text{x}=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has only $1$ pivot column. This implies that we will have only $2-1=1$ linearly independent eigenvector corresponding to the current eigenvalue. Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable.
